profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional hospital network is reviewing a proposed AMSTAR 2 appraisal module inside its internal evidence portal, which guideline analysts use to vet published systematic reviews before formulary and care-pathway decisions. The design review focuses on a Figma prototype and workflow spec for how analysts will enter AMSTAR 2 judgments, store supporting evidence, and generate a summary for committee packets. The agenda is to decide whether the design is ready for a three-week pilot, identify any gaps in handling reviews that include non-randomised intervention studies, and confirm what the pilot deliverable should look like. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the prototype with a short list of revisions before pilot launch.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Systematic review methods, health technology assessment, AMSTAR 2, GRADE
members.background: Former Cochrane methods editor who now leads evidence standards for the hospital network's clinical policy team.
members.private_state: She wants the tool to preserve methodological defensibility because committee decisions are sometimes audited, and she is worried that a streamlined interface could make weak appraisals look authoritative.
hidden_assumptions: "Ready for pilot" means two trained analysts could use the module on past reviews and reach reasonably consistent AMSTAR 2 judgments with enough rationale to defend them.

When people say "the protocol," they mean the earliest review protocol or methods document that establishes whether key methods were set before the review began, regardless of whether it is in PROSPERO, a supplement, or an internal appendix later published.
Even when the same passage supports multiple AMSTAR 2 items, each item should still have its own evidence note and rationale because the judgment logic is item-specific.
An AMSTAR 2 appraisal is not complete unless the output includes an exportable rationale summary suitable for a committee packet, not just item selections inside the app.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Workflow UX, regulated enterprise software, structured review forms
members.background: A UX lead who has designed submission and audit workflows for life-sciences and hospital operations platforms.
members.private_state: He wants approval without adding major scope because engineering capacity is fixed this quarter, and he is trying to keep the analyst workflow lightweight enough that teams will actually use it.
hidden_assumptions: "Ready for pilot" means analysts can complete the workflow end-to-end without blockers, excessive training, or obvious usability issues; methodological fine-tuning can follow from pilot feedback.

When people say "the protocol," they mean the single canonical protocol artifact the analyst selects in the case record, typically the PROSPERO entry or uploaded protocol PDF, rather than the system resolving among multiple versions.
If the same evidence passage is used across related questions, it should be captured once and linked to multiple AMSTAR 2 items to reduce friction and duplication.
The pilot scope is the in-app appraisal workflow; polished exports and committee-ready summary packets belong to a later reporting phase unless someone explicitly reopens scope.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design should be 'ready for pilot' next month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'ready for pilot' means the module is methodologically faithful enough that analysts can produce consistent, defensible AMSTAR 2 appraisals on real retrospective cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'ready for pilot' means the workflow is usable enough for analysts to complete appraisals without major UI blockers, even if some methodological refinements emerge during the pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'pilot-ready' sounds like a shared milestone term, and both members sincerely support running a pilot; the difference in acceptance standard hides behind the same scheduling language.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to reviewing 'the AMSTAR 2 output' for the committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the output includes an exportable rationale summary with item-level notes and the basis for the overall confidence rating, because that is what committee members will actually read.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the output is the completed in-app record plus overall confidence label, while narrative exports are outside the present design review and can be added later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same appraisal record and committee use case, so 'output' feels self-explanatory; neither pauses to separate the internal data capture artifact from the externally circulated packet.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss attaching 'the protocol' to judge whether methods were established before commencement.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of whichever earliest dated methods document truly anchors the review plan, including a supplement or appendix if it predates PROSPERO registration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of one designated protocol object in the system, usually the PROSPERO record or uploaded protocol file that the analyst chooses as the canonical reference.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Systematic reviews often have several closely related protocol artifacts with overlapping titles and dates, so both can say 'the protocol' without noticing they mean different concrete documents.

misalignment_points.topic: How evidence should be reused across related items
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree analysts should not have to 'enter the duplicate-process evidence twice.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means analysts can paste the same cited passage into separate item-specific rationale fields for the relevant AMSTAR 2 questions, preserving distinct judgments for study selection and data extraction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the system should collect one shared evidence block and propagate it across related AMSTAR 2 items so analysts only maintain it once.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to reduce redundant effort, so the phrase 'don't enter it twice' sounds aligned; the hidden disagreement is about whether reuse happens in the analyst's writing process or in the system's data structure.

turns.inner_thought: Before we sign off, I need confidence this is methodologically defensible, not just visually coherent. 'Ready for pilot' to me means two trained analysts can use it on prior reviews, including mixed bodies of randomised and non-randomised intervention studies, and land on reasonably consistent AMSTAR 2 judgments with enough rationale to withstand committee scrutiny or audit.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this framed around usability and scope discipline. turns.utterance: Sure. Here the analyst selects the protocol in the case record, and once that’s attached they can capture the registration date from that source and use it in the appraisal.

turns.inner_thought: The duplicate-process items are a classic place where oversimplification causes trouble. The same passage can support both study selection and data extraction, but each AMSTAR 2 item still needs its own evidence note and rationale because the judgment logic differs. Reuse is fine; collapsing the rationale is not.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On the duplicate-process questions, the same methods passage often supports both items, but analysts still need the reasoning to be clear for each AMSTAR 2 judgment. They shouldn’t have to enter the duplicate-process evidence twice.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on reducing friction. The prototype uses a shared evidence card that can feed multiple related items, so analysts maintain it once instead of copying it around. That's exactly the kind of lightweight pattern that will help adoption.
turns.utterance: Right, and that’s what the prototype is trying to do. We don’t want analysts to enter the duplicate-process evidence twice, so one evidence card can feed multiple related questions.

turns.inner_thought: If we do proceed, the pilot has to test whether the tool yields stable, defensible judgments on real retrospective cases and whether the committee packet remains usable. I want a small set of previously appraised reviews so we can compare analyst agreement and see whether the AMSTAR 2 output stands up in the actual governance context.

If reporting concerns surface, we can scope them after the trial.
